To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HIV-infected patients’ peripheral blood mononuciear cells exposed to the KVEIM antigen exhibit a reproducible antigen concentration-dependent cytokine response that is HIV group–specific, and that the cytokine response patterns are suggestive of a type 1-like response.
PBMCs from HIV-infected individuals, when exposed to the KVEIM antigen in vitro, exhibit a concentration-dependent proliferation and cytokine secretion.
the Kveim immunogen has the potential to modulate the immune system in the direction of a type 1 (Th1)-like response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of an immunogen that can modulate the production of cytokines and induce a type 1 (Th1)–like response in PBMCs harvested form HIV-infected individuals.
developing and testing a novel paradigm to modulate cytokine production and promote immune system reconstitution in HIV–acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
the development of a novel immunogen of human origin to modulate cytokine production in HIV–acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the data support the concept that a novel human immunogen, when used in a paradigm that focuses on immune system reconstitution and immunomodulation, may prove to be an important component in the development of an HIV–acquired immunodeficiency syndrome vaccine.
the Kveim test antigen is a novel immunogen that modulates cytokine production and promotes immune system reconstitution in HIV-infected patients.
this study demonstrates that the Kveim immunogen has immunomodulatory and immunoregulatory properties that may have therapeutic implications in HIV–acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Kveim immunogen is capable of modulating the immune response in a manner that is consistent with immune system reconstitution and the development of an HIV–acquired immunodeficiency syndrome vaccine.

we have demonstrated that PBMCs harvested form HIV-infected patients can be used to test a novel immunogen for the ability to modulate the immune system in a manner that is consistent with immune system reconstitution.

the Kveim test has a number of properties that make it an ideal candidate for use as an immunogen in a vaccine paradigm that emphasizes immunostimulation and immune system reconstuction as requisites to an effective human immunodefiency virus (HIV)—acquired immune deficiency virus vaccine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Kveim immunogen is capable of modulating the immune response of HIV-infected patients in the direction of an immune system reconstitution.
HIV-infected subjects can respond in an antigen concentration-dependent fashion to a novel immunogen.
the use of the Kveim test antigen in HIV–acquired immunodeficiency syndrome patients is feasible and may provide a means to modulate cytokine production in vivo.
